title: Latency stitching: exploratory notes on batcher heuristics and tail mitigation
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an exploratory experiment series where we attempted a lightweight technique we call 'latency stitching' to reduce P99/P999 tail latencies in the continuous batcher without dramatically lowering average throughput. The goal is a pragmatic set of heuristics we can prototype in the runtime as an alternative to heavy-handed preemption or strict priority queues.

Motivation / context:
- We see recurring microspikes in P99 under mixed-length workloads (short chat turns interleaved with multi-token generation).
- Existing approaches we tried (aggressive timeouts, strict urgency buckets) either hurt throughput or cause starvation of bulk requests.
- 'Latency stitching' is an idea to stitch short-window flushes into longer batch formation so that short requests can be carved out predictably while preserving batch benefits for long requests.

High-level description:
- Maintain the normal continuous coalescer. Add a light-weight short-window stitcher that:
  1) allows an occasional short flush (e.g., 2-5ms) targeted at slots with high short-request concentration,
  2) when performing a short flush, we opportunistically prefill the active batch with low-cost placeholders (no-op prefills) so kernel hotpaths see fewer tiny kernels,
  3) stitch results back into the main completion stream via the normal kv-cache semantics.
- Key constraint: minimal code-path divergence from the main batcher to keep instrumentation simple and low-risk.

Hypotheses:
H1: Short, frequent stitches will reduce tail for tiny requests (P95-P99) without reducing normalized throughput more than 5%.
H2: Placeholder prefilling will reduce kernel overhead amplification from tiny kernels and therefore keep GPU efficiency higher than naive short flushes.
H3: Uncoordinated stitches across slots cause oscillation; a dampening/backoff layer will stabilize behavior.

Experiment plan:
- Workloads: three replays from production traces: 
  A) chat-heavy (median tokens=8, 15% long tails >256 tokens)
  B) mixed (bi-modal, short and long)
  C) bulk-inference (mostly long requests).
- Baselines: current continuous coalescer (v3) tuned with default timeouts; also baseline aggressive timeout (10ms).
- Variables: stitch-window (2, 5, 10 ms), stitch-frequency cap (1 per slot per 50ms, 1 per 5ms, disabled), prefill-size (0, 4, 8 placeholders), backoff damping factor (0.2, 0.5, 0.9).
- Metrics: P50/P90/P95/P99/P999, throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec), GPU utilization, kernel launch rate, average batch size, fairness index (per-tenant P95 ratio), cost-per-token proxy.
- Measurement method: deterministic replay on 4-GPU test cluster with perf counters + microtraces enabled. 30-minute steady window per config, repeated 3x.

Results (summary):
- Best config: stitch-window=5ms, frequency cap=1 per slot per 50ms, prefill-size=4, damping=0.5.
  - Chat-heavy: P99 reduced ~28% (280ms -> 205ms), P999 reduced ~22%, throughput drop ~3%, kernel launch rate down 12% vs naive short flush.
  - Mixed: P99 reduced ~18%, throughput drop ~4.5%.
  - Bulk-inference: negligible change in P99, throughput impact <1% when stitcher kept mostly idle.
- Naive short flush (2ms, no prefill): P99 improved but kernel launch rate skyrocketed (~+60%) and GPU utilization fell by ~8% leading to 10-12% throughput loss on long-running workloads.
- Prefill effect: adding small prefill (4 placeholders) reduced kernel launch rate by ~25% relative to no-prefill stitches and recovered about half the throughput loss.
- Damping: with no damping there was slot-level oscillation (periodic over-flushing) that inverted fairness in some tenants. Damping=0.5 stabilized and kept fairness index within acceptable bounds.

Profiling observations / bottlenecks:
- Kernel amortization is the dominant factor: many tiny kernels suffer high fixed latency per launch on our GPU stack. Prefill reduces number of tiny kernels by merging tiny requests into slightly larger kernels.
- KV cache serialization accounted for ~6-10% of the per-request CPU overhead when stitches were frequent; need to micro-optimize serialization path.
- Scheduler contention: lock contention rose under high stitch frequencies (hot slots). Moving the stitch decision to an async sampler helped but added complexity.

Failure modes / safety notes:
- Excessive stitches can hurt long-request latency catastrophically if stitch policy is mis-configured (we observed P50 inflation in one misconfigured run).
- Prefill placeholders must be implemented as zero-cost or very cheap ops; any heavy placeholder work erases benefit.
- Cross-slot coordination is necessary for multi-tenant fairness. Undefined interaction with quota enforcers caused temporary quota overshoot in one run.

Actionable next steps:
- Short term (prototype): land a guarded feature flag with the best config; add telemetry hooks (stitch counts per-slot, kernel launches per-stitch, per-tenant fairness metrics). Owner: Jordan, PR: #2093.
- Mid term: refactor kv-cache serialization to reduce stitch-induced CPU overhead; explore lock-free sampling for stitch decisions. Owner: Avery.
- Long term: evaluate a hybrid strategy that combines stitching with conservative preemption for emergency SLOs. Owner: Samir.

Open questions / notes-to-self:
- How do stitches interact with function/tool-calls that require structured output? Need to ensure no ordering regressions.
- Edge case: multi-token streaming responses that are already producing partial outputs — stitching could duplicate partial state; add explicit idempotency checks.
- Can we derive per-deployment default configs using a short 2-minute warmup trace sampler? Would save ops vs manual tuning.

Appendix: key microtraces (short summary)
- Trace A (chat-heavy): saw 3 distinct microburst clusters at t=120s/350s/410s. Stitches smoothed cluster peaks but introduced a minor shift in completion ordering; harmless in our tests.
- Trace B (mixed): two-phase behavior: initial short requests followed by a sustained long-request wave. Stitcher needs to back off automatically when long wave detected.

References / links:
- Linear ticket: RT-1426 (experiment coordination)
- Draft PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2093
- Related: microburst-queue-occupancy-and-preemption-tradeoffs (drive notes)

TL;DR:
Latency stitching looks promising as a low-risk mitigation for short-request tails. The sweet spot requires small prefills and sensible damping. The prototype reduces P99 with single-digit throughput loss on mixed workloads and negligible impact on bulk workloads. Next step: feature-flagged runtime prototype + telemetry, then a controlled canary on Dedicated.

Notes (informal):
- This doc is intentionally exploratory; experiments are noisy. Treat numbers as directional.
- Would be good to run one more sweep with alternate GPUs (A100 -> H100) to see kernel launch cost differences.
